overview: Picture a kingdom as a chain of guarded mountain gates: Kabul behind high passes, fertile Swat beyond watchtowers, and Hund beside the rushing Indus. The rulers now called Hindu Shahis inherited this crossroads around 822 CE and gradually shifted east as Saffarid and Ghaznavid power squeezed their western lands. In the atlas, however, hindu-shahis exists only from 900 to 1000, misses Kabul, Peshawar, Hund and Swat, and floats across part of the Punjab. The historical story is bigger. Lalliya, Kamalavarman, Bhima Deva and Jayapala ruled through forts, alliances, inscriptions, temples and widely circulating coins. Jayapala fought Sebüktegin and Mahmud; Anandapala, Trilocanapala and Bhimapala continued after the atlas erased their id. By about 1026 or 1027 the dynasty ended under Ghaznavid conquest. Archaeology recovers straight streets, kitchens, bathrooms, drains, wells, dice and tiny beads, while honest gaps remain about ordinary children, healers and household toilets.

periods.title: Lalliya and an atlas window begin at different moments
periods.summary: The Late Shahi line had already ruled for decades. Around 900, Lalliya was associated with Udabhanda or Hund, while Kashmir intervened in a succession that brought his son Kamalavarman to power.

periods.title: Kamalavarman rules from an Indus-facing political world
periods.summary: Kamalavarman, also called Kamalu or Kamaluka in different sources, inherited a realm tied to Gandhara, Udabhanda and Kashmir. Names and dates are reconstructed by comparing chronicles, inscriptions and coins.

periods.title: Bhima Deva appears in stone
periods.summary: The damaged Dewai inscription names Bhima Deva and his father Kamalavarman. Its high titles advertise authority, but the text alone cannot draw a border or reveal how evenly royal commands reached each valley.

periods.title: Bhima Deva joins power, worship and family diplomacy
periods.summary: Bhima was remembered at Udabhanda, linked to a Vishnu temple and connected by marriage to the ruling house of Kashmir. Those elite ties supported politics but do not describe every family in the realm.

periods.title: Jayapala rules a network of fortified places
periods.summary: Jayapala is named at Hund and probably in the fragmentary Barikot record, where three people helped restore a religious building. Inscriptions locate royal names and patrons more securely than any modern-looking frontier.

periods.title: Pressure builds from Ghazni
periods.summary: Sebüktegin consolidated power at Ghazni while Jayapala watched the western approaches. Mountain roads, forts and river valleys mattered because armies, messengers and supplies had to move through them.

periods.title: Jayapala and Sebüktegin fight along the Kabul River corridor
periods.summary: Sebüktegin campaigned through Laghman toward Peshawar and defeated Jayapala twice. Court histories magnify victories, so the secure conclusion is territorial pressure and loss, not every colorful speech later attached to the wars.

periods.title: Mahmud rises as the atlas prepares to erase the Shahis
periods.summary: Mahmud succeeded at Ghazni in 998 and soon renewed attacks eastward. The atlas ends hindu-shahis at 1000, yet Jayapala and three successors continued resistance until about 1026 or 1027.

sections.title: First, test the map against the kingdom

items.text: The exact imported record is id “hindu-shahis,” name “Hindu Shahis,” circa 900 to 1000. It was missing a card and researched override. Kingdom of Kapisa, Kingdom of Kashmir, Saffarids, Samanids and Ghaznavids are separate records, so this card cannot quietly absorb or overwrite them.

At 900 the target is one Polygon with one ring and 14 positions. Its bounds are 71.700° to 79.149° east and 28.336° to 33.346° north; coordinate SHA-256 is 5be7f04275d2d1f39b061cb9ececf79104c5691ab986e7badae71f9b3afc9b12. Nandana, Katas, Lahore and Sialkot test inside.

The same polygon excludes Kabul, Kapisa, Ghazni, Laghman, Peshawar, Hund, Taxila, Barikot, Udegram, Swat, Bilot, Bannu, Chitral, Srinagar and Multan. Missing Hund and Barikot is especially serious because inscriptions, archaeology and texts directly connect those places to Late Shahi rulers.

At 900 the atlas assigns every tested secure center from Kabul through Hund and Swat to samanid-empire, while hindu-shahis occupies a southern Punjab shape. This is not a small fuzzy-edge problem. The two layers place the dynasty outside much of its best-attested political and archaeological landscape.

The target is absent at 700, 800, 1000, 1100 and 1200. Kingdom of Kapisa covers the Kabul and Swat tests in 700; a broad Abbasid layer covers them in 800; Ghaznavids cover Kabul by 1000. Premodern power followed forts, roads and alliances, so these abrupt atlas blocks are illustrations, not surveyed borders.

sections.title: A name, a takeover and rulers reconstructed from scraps

items.text: “Hindu Shahis” is a modern standard label built largely from al-Biruni’s phrase for the later “Shahis of al-Hind.” Recent scholarship often says Late Shahis because religion did not flip like a switch and the realm contained Hindu, Buddhist and Muslim communities. The atlas id stays exact even while the card explains that history.

Al-Biruni says Kallara was a Brahmin minister who imprisoned Lagaturman and took the kingship after finding treasure and gaining power. He wrote about two centuries later and shaped the event as a moral tale. Archaeologists cautiously place the transition around 822, rather than treating every detail as eyewitness reporting.

Lalliya, probably ruling from about 870 to 902, is associated by the Rajatarangini with Udabhanda beside the Indus. The name may connect with Samanta Deva coin issues, but titles on coins do not map neatly onto personal names in chronicles. Matching them is a scholarly hypothesis, not a solved name tag.

Kamalavarman appears under several names: Kamalu in al-Biruni, Kamaluka or Toramana in the Kashmiri chronicle, and Kamalavarman in the Dewai inscription. Different languages and literary purposes preserved different forms. Historians align them by sequence and family connections while admitting that the chronology remains putative.

Bhima Deva, approximately 921 to 964, receives a mountain of titles on the Dewai stone: great king over kings, supreme lord and Shahi. Such language tells us how a court wanted power to sound. It does not prove that Bhima personally controlled every place where later maps draw a solid color.

sections.title: Jayapala faces Ghazni, and the line survives the map seam

items.text: Jayapala saw the new power at Ghazni as a threat and fought Sebüktegin in the 980s. Sebüktegin moved through Laghman toward Peshawar and defeated him twice. Later narratives supply speeches, storms and moral lessons; the safer history is repeated war, frontier loss and a shifting balance west of the Indus.

Mahmud defeated Jayapala in 1001, just after the atlas removes the Shahi layer. Older accounts say Jayapala abdicated and died by fire from shame. Because those motives come through courtly historical traditions, the card labels the reported self-immolation instead of entering the king’s mind as if a camera were present.

Anandapala succeeded and helped assemble a broad coalition against Mahmud. The coalition lost near Peshawar or Waihind in 1008. A famous story blames panic after Anandapala’s elephant bolted, but battle tales often compress chaos into one dramatic animal; alliances, terrain and organization mattered too.

Trilocanapala ruled after about 1010 and sought Kashmiri military help. Kalhana’s later chronicle praises his courage while criticizing allied commanders. This shows active diplomacy and fighting after the atlas endpoint, but it is also a literary account written for Kashmir, not a neutral battlefield report.

Al-Biruni lists Trilocanapala’s death in 1021 or 1022 and Bhimapala five years later. Iranica dates the final ending to 1026. The bundle uses circa 1027 to reflect the conversion and source uncertainty, then links the territorial conquest to ghaznavid-emirate without claiming every community changed overnight.

sections.title: Kings, local patrons, alliances and a wall of watchtowers

items.text: Royal inscriptions display elaborate hierarchy, but administration below the king is only patchily visible. At Barikot, a fragment names Jayapala and three people who patronized reconstruction of a devakula, a religious building. Local action and royal time appear together without proving the project was ordered or paid for by the king.

Udabhanda, now Hund, stood at an Indus crossing and is repeatedly called the town or capital of Gandhara in early medieval sources. Its location made it useful for courts, travelers and armies. “Capital” still should not be imagined as one permanent modern ministry building governing every mountain valley by paperwork.

In Swat, archaeologists trace a planned defensive system of hilltop fortresses, smaller garrison forts and watchtowers along roads and passes. These guarded fertile land, water and movement. A tower could warn a valley faster than a distant palace, making geography part of government rather than scenery behind it.

Castle cities such as Udegram and Barikot squeezed dense settlement onto defended slopes, often with a hilltop citadel and a Brahmanical temple. Springs and wells helped people endure inside. Archaeologists use “palace” or “castle” cautiously because ruined walls rarely arrive with room labels.

Marriage linked Shahi and Kashmiri elites. Bhima Deva’s granddaughter Didda married the Kashmiri king Kshemagupta, and the kingdoms exchanged military aid. This is evidence for dynastic family strategy at the top. It cannot be stretched into a rule for how farmers, artisans or servants chose partners.

sections.title: Roads, harvests, markets and money with a bull

items.text: Routes ran east from Kabul along the Kabul River and through the Khyber approaches, while alternatives crossed the Kurram and Tochi valleys toward the Indus. None was an effortless highway. Narrow passes, snow, mud, river crossings and raiders shaped the cost and season of moving armies, letters, pilgrims and goods.

Swat’s well-watered loess soils supported reliable double cropping compared with drier plains that depended more heavily on the monsoon. Forts concentrated around this productive landscape. The evidence supports valuable harvests and storage, but it does not turn the entire Shahi realm into one identical green farm.

Late Shahi silver coins usually show Shiva’s bull Nandi beneath a Proto-Sharada legend and a spear-holding horseman on the other face. Copper series could show an elephant and lion. The designs joined religious and military signals in pocket-sized objects, though users did not need to read every letter to recognize the type.

The earliest Late Shahi silver issues weighed about four grams, later settling near three to 3.1 grams. XRF tests show changing silver and intentionally added copper, but metal percentages do not identify one mine with certainty. A coin can reveal policy and resources without confessing exactly where its ore began.

Coin finds cluster in Kabulistan, Uddiyana and Gandhara, with especially strong archaeological evidence from places such as Barikot and Udegram. Their spread marks payment and movement, not a perfectly outlined empire. Wider early medieval markets also exchanged grain, cloth, animals, salt and craft goods through routes and towns.

sections.title: Temples that mixed building traditions and living religions

items.text: Salt Range temples combined northern Indian Nagara forms with older Gandharan habits and Iranian-related true arches, domes and vaults. Builders cut porous kanjur into regular courses, used mortar, then covered walls with lime plaster and color. The result was local invention from several traditions, not a copied architecture kit.

At Barikot, a Shahi temple stood high above a steep stair and probably rose more than twelve meters from its floor. Its rubble core, retaining walls, cut stone and plaster required planners, quarry workers, carriers and masons. Monumental height also controlled the visitor’s first view like careful stage scenery.

Hindu worship became prominent, with temples dedicated to Shiva, Vishnu and other deities, but Buddhist objects and institutions did not instantly vanish. Kabul and Gandhara also included Muslim communities. A dynastic nickname cannot make every subject share one belief, and religious change unfolded differently from place to place.

Shahi-period sculptors made sacred figures in marble, stucco, copper alloys and clay. Red-clay artists built a core around a wooden peg, pressed faces in molds, modeled hair by hand and attached tiny ornaments. What looks magically lifelike began with recipes, armatures, fingers and many chances for the nose to go crooked.

Copper-alloy images used varied alloys, casting choices and surface treatments. Researchers cannot yet assign every statue to a workshop from chemistry alone because makers remelted metal and selected mixtures for color, hardness or easier casting. Technical skill is real; a neat factory label would be less real.

sections.title: A stone voice, a coin label and lessons for princes

items.text: Most Late Shahi inscriptions use Sanskrit in Proto-Sharada, with Sharada emerging around the eleventh century. Scripts traveled beyond dynastic borders and served royal praise, donations, land records, religious formulas and even graffiti. Writing culture was varied, so one inscription style cannot be called everybody’s handwriting.

Authentic sample from the damaged Dewai inscription, in readable modern Devanagari normalization: “परमभट्टारक-महाराजाधिराज-परमेश्वर-शाहि-श्री-भीमदेवः”. The original is tenth-century Sanskrit in Proto-Sharada characters. This display supplies letters restored by editors and changes scripts for readability; it is not a tracing of the stone.

Transliteration: “paramabhaṭṭāraka-mahārājādhirāja-parameśvara-śāhi-śrī-bhīmadevaḥ”. Translation: “the supreme venerable great king over kings, supreme lord, Shahi, illustrious Bhima Deva.” This is formal royal titulature, not a greeting heard in an ordinary kitchen, and each grand title describes a claim to rank rather than measured territory.

Coin legends offered shorter writing. One common series reads “śrī sāmanta deva,” normalized as “श्री सामन्तदेव,” meaning “Illustrious Samanta Deva.” Scholars increasingly treat Samanta Deva as a title shared across issues rather than one securely identified king. A British Museum example is only ten millimeters wide.

Al-Biruni says grammarian Ugrabhuti taught Prince Anandapala and sent his completed book to Kashmir. Anandapala supported its learned reception with gifts. This is unusually direct evidence for an elite teacher, pupil and manuscript network. It says nothing certain about whether a potter’s daughter attended a formal school.

sections.title: Families, ranks and what childhood sources forgot

items.text: Royal genealogy makes some elite women visible: Didda was Bhima Deva’s granddaughter and became queen in Kashmir. Her marriage connected ruling houses, but the sources name her because she mattered to dynastic politics. They rarely preserve a shepherd mother’s choices, a craftswoman’s authority or a grandmother’s stories.

Early medieval society used Brahmanical varna ideals alongside many local jatis, occupations and negotiated ranks. Court service, land, craft, gender and religious status shaped opportunity. These categories were not a tidy four-row classroom chart, and evidence written by elites reveals hierarchy more readily than ordinary people speaking for themselves.

At Hund, gates opened from houses onto streets laid at right angles, suggesting households lived within an organized neighborhood. Rooms, halls, ovens and repeated floors show activity through time. Archaeology finds spaces and objects, though it cannot tell whether each room held a nuclear family, relatives, servants, tenants or several combinations.

Children are almost invisible in written Shahi records. Miniature pots, terracotta animals, ivory dice and pendants were excavated at Hund, but context and purpose vary: some might relate to play, ritual, teaching or adult use. Calling every small object a toy would make a charming museum label and weak archaeology.

Most learning probably happened through participation: speaking local languages, helping with animals or food, observing craft steps and memorizing religious or family knowledge. That is a careful inference from household and occupational life, not a surviving Shahi timetable. Formal Sanskrit study is securely visible mainly among princes, scribes and learned specialists.

sections.title: Homes, bowls, jewelry, work and a handful of game pieces

items.text: Hund’s excavators found rooms and halls built in stone masonry, often with pebble or slab floors. Its pottery included bowls, cups, pitchers, jars, lamps, cooking pots, storage vessels and plates. That gives a sturdy household toolkit, although one excavation area cannot furnish every mountain village in exactly the same style.

Cooking pots, ovens, storage jars, sickle fragments and millstones connect meals to harvesting, storing, grinding and heating. Swat’s double-crop fields could feed towns and travelers. The evidence does not preserve a Late Shahi cookbook, so the card stops at grain foods and varied local produce instead of inventing tonight’s stew.

Gold earrings, hundreds of beads, bangles, rings, antimony rods and pendants show adornment at Hund. Beads used carnelian, lapis, agate, glass, clay, bone and ivory. Textiles rarely survived there, so clothing is reconstructed cautiously from sculptures showing tunics, shawls and jewelry, not as one uniform for everyone.

Work left sharper clues: sickles for harvesting, knives and axes for cutting, nails and bars for building, arrowheads for weapons, and weight cubes or cowries for exchange. Wider early medieval production relied on skilled practice and unequal labor. A tool names a task more readily than the worker’s age, pay or legal status.

Barikot’s later medieval fill contained clay dice and dozens of board-game tokens cut from pottery or stone, while Hund produced ivory dice. Some deposits were dumped during the Ghaznavid phase, so the pieces show regional play around the Shahi transition rather than a game securely owned by one Shahi child. The rules are lost.

sections.title: Health, water, bathrooms, toilets and what continued

items.text: The wider Susruta tradition discusses anatomy, surgery, remedies and learning from a teacher, but its textual layers and dates are debated. It supplies South Asian medical background, not a patient chart from Hund. Direct evidence for Shahi physicians, midwives, household caregivers and access to treatment remains frustratingly sparse.

Antimony rods from Hund may have served eye cosmetic or medicinal preparation, yet the object alone cannot choose between beauty, health or both. Knives are equally unsafe to relabel as surgical tools without context. Archaeology rewards careful verbs: an implement was found; its exact user and purpose may remain unknown.

Water systems were serious infrastructure. Hund had a stone-ringed well; Swat forts enclosed springs and masonry wells; Barikot raised water from a deep couloir to a cistern; another fortified center had three springs, a large well and a stepped tank. Drinking, cooking, ritual, washing and defense could all depend on maintenance.

Hund’s pre-Muslim buildings included bathrooms paved with long watertight slabs. Drains carried water into the main street, sometimes into large sewerage pots beneath the outlets. This is unusually direct sanitation evidence, though the report groups several pre-Muslim phases and does not identify an ordinary household latrine or a flushing toilet.

Ghaznavid conquest ended the Shahi ruling line around 1026 or 1027, but people, fields, roads, coin habits, temples and craft knowledge continued. At 1000 the atlas had already erased the exact id; by 1100 it redraws the region again. A dynasty can end while a potter still opens the workshop next morning.

ending.text: After Jayapala, Anandapala and Trilocanapala fought a long defensive struggle, al-Biruni places Bhimapala’s death five years after 1021 or 1022. Modern syntheses therefore end the Late Shahi line around 1026 or 1027. Ghaznavid rule took the main territorial core, especially the western Punjab, but Kashmir ties, religious communities, fortified settlements, farms, waterworks, coin designs and craft practices did not vanish in one year. This card records conquest at circa 1027 and names ghaznavid-emirate as the political successor, while keeping the atlas’s premature 1000 disappearance visible as a separate data problem.
